title: Foreign Money Is Leaving India's Stock Market at a Record Pace. For the First Time in Two Decades, Indian Investors Don't Need It.
excerpt: The RBI's latest Financial Stability Report reveals FPI ownership at a 20-year low of 16%, with domestic investors commanding 20% — and new rules now let NRIs own even more.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • FPI ownership in Indian equities has dropped to a 20-year low of 16%.
  • Domestic investors now hold 20% of the market, marking a historic shift.
  • In 2026, FPIs withdrew ₹2.7 lakh crore, surpassing last year's record outflow.
  • Indian mutual fund assets have surged to ₹60 lakh crore since 2020.
  • New RBI rules allow NRIs greater access to Indian equity markets.

For decades, the direction of India's stock market was decided thousands of miles away — in the trading desks of New York, London, and Singapore. When foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) bought, the market surged. When they sold, it crashed. That era, the Reserve Bank of India's latest data suggests, is ending. According to the RBI's Financial Stability Report released on June 30, FPI ownership of Indian equities has fallen to 16 per cent as of March 2026 — a two-decade low. In the same period, domestic institutional investors (DIIs) have climbed to 20 per cent, marking the widest gap in history between the two. For the first time in over 20 years, India's markets are being run primarily by Indian money. ## The Scale of the Exit The numbers are staggering. FPIs have pulled ₹2.7 lakh crore ($31 billion) out of Indian equities so far in 2026, already surpassing the ₹1.66 lakh crore ($19 billion) they withdrew in all of 2025 — which was itself a record. In June alone, foreign investors withdrew ₹49,340 crore ($5.16 billion), according to data from the Central Depository Services (India) Ltd. Every month of 2026 except February has seen net FPI selling. March was the worst, with a record ₹1.17 lakh crore outflow. April saw ₹60,847 crore leave, May lost ₹32,963 crore, and June added another ₹49,340 crore to the tally. The assets under custody held by FPIs in the equity segment fell from roughly ₹74 lakh crore in December to about ₹68 lakh crore by May — a decline of ₹6 lakh crore, driven primarily by valuation losses of ₹5 lakh crore and net outflows of about ₹2 lakh crore, per the FSR. ## Why Foreign Money Is Leaving Multiple forces are at work. Himanshu Srivastava of Morningstar attributed June's outflows to "global risk aversion in the first half, continued preference for developed markets, higher US yields, and valuation concerns around Indian equities." > **"March was the worst, with a record ₹1.17 lakh crore outflow."** A critical factor is the AI trade. South Korea and Taiwan — home to the world's leading chip and memory manufacturers — have been siphoning FPI capital away from India, which lacks a comparable presence in the artificial intelligence hardware supply chain. V K Vijayakumar of Geojit Investments noted that heavy FPI profit-booking in those volatile Asian markets also contributed to the moderation in India selling later in June. India's earnings growth differential compared to other emerging markets has slipped below its long-term average, the FSR noted, and valuations — while corrected from their 2024 highs — remain at the upper end of historical ranges, particularly for midcap and smallcap stocks. About two-thirds of listed stocks were trading above their benchmark P/E ratios as of March 2025. The Iran-Gulf conflict's fallout added another headwind. The RBI warned that elevated crude oil prices could widen India's current account deficit and put pressure on the fiscal arithmetic — though energy prices corrected sharply after the US-Iran truce deal in late June. ## The Domestic Wall But here is the structural transformation the headline FPI numbers obscure: India's domestic investors have become the market's shock absorbers. DII ownership has more than doubled from 13.58 per cent in 2020 to 20 per cent in 2026. The engine behind this is the mutual fund revolution. Indian mutual fund assets under management crossed ₹60 lakh crore, up from ₹22 lakh crore in 2020, according to the Association of Mutual Funds in India. Systematic Investment Plans (SIPs) — the monthly auto-invest mechanism that has become a household habit for middle-class Indians — are pumping in over ₹25,000 crore every single month. Add institutional flows from the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) and the Life Insurance Corporation (LIC), and the result is a deep, steady pool of domestic capital that barely flinches when foreigners sell. "When FPIs pulled out nearly ₹1 trillion, our markets barely flinched because ₹1.07 trillion of domestic money stepped in, absorbing the shock like a sponge," noted analysts at Geojit. "For the first time in 15 years, Indian mutual funds and pension schemes, not foreign investors, are calling the shots." Pranav Haldea, Managing Director of PRIME Database Group, called it a "landmark moment" for the Indian capital market. "Indian markets shall continue their steadfast march towards even more 'atmanirbharta' in the quarters and years to follow," he said.

## What This Means for the Diaspora The RBI's response to the FPI exodus has a direct bearing on NRIs. Among the measures announced in June to attract overseas capital, the central bank specifically **raised investment limits for non-resident Indians and overseas citizens of India in domestic equities**. Other steps include the RBI absorbing hedging costs on FCNR (Foreign Currency Non-Resident) deposits and expanding the forex swap window. For India's approximately 18 million NRIs worldwide, these changes translate into broader access to India's equity markets — at a time when valuations have corrected from their peaks and domestic fundamentals remain sound. India's GDP grew 7.7 per cent in FY26, and the banking system's capital ratios remain well above regulatory thresholds even under adverse stress scenarios, the FSR noted. The shift also carries a psychological dimension. For years, NRI investors watched FPI flows as the primary signal for India market timing. With domestic capital now dominant, the playbook changes: India's markets increasingly move on Indian fundamentals — monsoon progress, GST collections, SIP flows — rather than the Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions. ## The Risks That Remain The FSR was careful not to frame this as a pure-positive story. It warned that FPIs' portfolio allocation to India within their emerging market funds was moderating, suggesting the shift isn't entirely driven by India-specific selling but also by a broader rebalancing away from emerging markets. Earnings forecasts, the report noted, are yet to fully reflect the geopolitical tensions and tariff uncertainties that could compress valuations further. There are also signs that DII ammunition, while substantial, isn't infinite. CLSA analysts warned that "the first signs of depletion in the resources of DIIs" were emerging — cash held by equity mutual funds stood at ₹1.78 trillion at the end of February 2026, down 24 per cent from April 2025. And FPI selling at this scale does carry macro consequences. Foreign portfolio flows remain critical for financing India's current account deficit. A prolonged exodus could pressure the rupee and force the RBI into defending the currency at the cost of reserves. But for now, the direction is clear: the era of foreign investors dictating terms to India's markets is over. The money leaving India's stock market is being replaced, rupee for rupee, by Indian capital — much of it from ordinary Indians investing ₹500 or ₹1,000 a month through SIPs. In the long arc of India's financial history, that may matter more than any single quarter of FPI outflows. *Sources: RBI Financial Stability Report (June 2026), CDSL, Hindu Business Line, Morningstar Investment Research India, PRIME Database Group, AMFI, CLSA*
